Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Nigeria Video shows hundreds held captive after Nigeria mosque kidnapping Gunmen ‌attacked worshippers in Dekara village on Friday taking women, children and older people Reuters in Maidiguri Mon 24 Aug 2026 10.19 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 10.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An armed group has posted a video showing what ⁠residents said were about ⁠600 women, children and ​older people abducted in an attack on a mosque in Nigeria’s north-central Niger State last week. The video, posted on Facebook and WhatsApp, ⁠showed large groups of people seated in a forested area surrounded by armed men. Several children could be heard crying in the background. Mass kidnappings for ransom have become common in ⁠parts of north-western and north-central Nigeria, where heavily armed gangs frequently raid villages, schools and highways and hold them until ​paid large sums of money. The violence was previously focused in the north of the country, but gunmen have ‌increasingly moved south. How rampant violence made Nigeria an insecurity hotspot in the Sahel – mapped Read more The video surfaced two days after the latest kidnapping, when gunmen ‌attacked worshippers at the mosque in Dekara village during Friday prayers, taking people away in what residents said were simultaneous raids on several communities. In the video, a gunman speaking in Hausa addressed families of the captives and urged them to identify relatives among the people in the footage. “These are all your people. We are showing you this video so that you can identify your family members, your fathers, mothers, children ‌and relatives,” the gunman said. Reuters could not verify the exact date or the location where the video was filmed. However, no older version of the video was found posted ​online before Sunday. Four residents said they were able to confirm the identities of some of those seized. “The people in the video are from Dekara. I’ve identified 13 people that I know,” Ibrahim Abubakar said. Another resident, Abdulmutallib Muqaddas Dindi, said those who appeared in the video had been seized during the prayers. “We have ⁠identified our elders, relatives, and some of us have seen their wives and children ​in the video,” he said. Police ​and state authorities did not respond ​to requests for comment on Monday. Police had earlier confirmed an attack on worshippers in ​the area but said ‌they could not ​verify the number of people ​abducted. Jamilu Ibrahim, another resident, appealed to the federal and state authorities to secure the release of the captives, pointing out the number of mothers with infants and children among those shown in the footage. http://www.bgnes.com/politics/hungary-ma.text: Despite objections from EU leaders, Hungary’s new government has decided to retain the state of emergency imposed over the threat of illegal migration. The special legal regime was first introduced by the previous government in 2016. Prime Minister Péter Magyar said no compromise had yet been reached with Brussels and that the state of emergency would remain in force at least until the end of the year. “The Tisza government will not relax the legal provisions concerning illegal migration. Recent weeks have shown that even the smallest legislative changes can create vulnerabilities in the protection of Europe’s external borders,” Magyar said in a statement issued in Budapest. After reviewing the situation, the government decided to extend the state of emergency due to mass migration until December 31, 2026. The measure had been due to expire on September 7. Magyar said Budapest had been negotiating with Brussels for several months over new Hungarian rules that would effectively protect Hungary’s and the EU’s external borders without violating European law. “So far, the EU institutions and legal experts have been unable to propose a solution that would allow the Hungarian authorities to continue acting with the required strictness and effectiveness,” the prime minister said. He also confirmed that his government would seek to overturn a 2024 ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union ordering Hungary to pay a €1 million fine for refusing to comply with EU rules concerning refugees and migrants. Magyar’s government, which took office following the April 12 parliamentary election, continues to reject EU migration requirements, following the approach of its predecessors. The state of emergency, repeatedly extended by Viktor Orbán’s government over the past decade, provides for strict measures against undocumented migrants. | BGNES

https://baltic-review.com/lithuania-nati.text: Share Tweet 0 The National Museum of Lithuania is opening branches in four locations without admission charges on 27 September 2026. The National Museum of Lithuania is turning the last Sunday of September into a nationwide invitation to explore history and culture. On 27 September 2026, visitors will be admitted free of charge to the museum’s branches in Vilnius, Palanga, Ožkabaliai and Kudirkos Naumiestis, according to an announcement published on 25 September. The initiative brings together a broad range of exhibitions rather than focusing on a single anniversary or collection. The programme moves from archaeology and the history of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania to high technology, book art, textile work and contemporary audiovisual installations. It also gives visitors a final opportunity to see several temporary exhibitions before they close. A museum network rather than a single venue In Vilnius, the museum’s House of Histories offers access to an ethnographic storage exhibition presenting objects connected with Lithuanian everyday life in earlier centuries. The same site is also showing “Trajectory of the Future: The History of Lithuania’s High-Tech Sector”, an exhibition that links scientific achievement with the country’s longer history. Its presentation includes themes ranging from biotechnology and lasers to space research, as well as an area devoted to Lithuanian video games. At Gediminas Castle Tower, the new “Frequency of Freedom” exposition considers Lithuania’s recurring experiences of resistance, responsibility and collective action. The museum presents these subjects not simply as a chronological sequence, but as questions about how communities respond to historical change. From the hill, visitors can also see Davide Rivalta’s bronze sculpture “Wolf” and the city below. Other Vilnius branches add different perspectives. The Castellan’s House presents “Understanding Lithuania”, a permanent exhibition organised around six themes, including creativity, beliefs, global connections and historical turning points. At the Old Arsenal, the archaeology exhibition “Reusable” examines how earlier communities repaired, adapted and repurposed objects—an approach that gives the idea of sustainability a long historical background. Final chances for book and archaeology exhibitions Sunday is also the closing day for “The Unknown Jonas Basanavičius: The Lithuanian Indiana Jones” at the House of Signatories. Created by archaeology master’s students from Vilnius University, the exhibition looks at Basanavičius not only as a national revival figure, but also as an archaeologist and anthropologist whose interests extended into the study of ancient burial sites. At the Kazys Varnelis House-Museum, two book-related exhibitions are reaching their final day. “Book Dragon. A Fantastic Story About the Beauty of Books” introduces visitors to bookmaking through interactive elements, including a printing press. “Book Art: The Most Beautiful Books of Lithuania and the Czech Republic” brings together award-winning titles from recent Lithuanian and Czech competitions. The museum is also offering free guided tours devoted to the optical art of Kazys Varnelis, although advance registration is required. The city’s official cultural-events calendar separately lists the two book exhibitions as running until 27 September, reinforcing the museum’s notice about the final opportunity to see them. The combination of free entry and closing-day programming gives the Sunday a practical appeal for both regular museum-goers and visitors who have not yet encountered the exhibitions. Culture beyond the capital The free-access programme extends beyond Vilnius. In Palanga, the Jonas Šliūpas Museum is presenting tapestries and paintings by Marija Švažienė, alongside a sensory exhibition about Lithuanian partisan history designed for both blind and sighted visitors. The display uses reconstructed objects that visitors can touch, try on or wear. At the Jonas Basanavičius birthplace in Ožkabaliai, the museum is connecting biography and contemporary art. The audiovisual installation “Es humanus” combines textiles, moving projections and music, while other exhibitions examine Basanavičius as a cultural organiser, scholar and physician. Outdoor displays, a film pavilion and a playroom for younger visitors broaden the site beyond a conventional house museum. In Kudirkos Naumiestis, visitors can explore the vanished town of Schirwindt through household objects, tools and other historical materials. A guided town walk at 1 p.m. is intended to connect the exhibition with the local urban landscape, including interwar modernist architecture and the overlapping histories of two neighbouring towns. By opening four locations without an admission fee, the National Museum of Lithuania is presenting culture as a network of places and experiences rather than a single central attraction. The Sunday programme combines permanent displays, temporary exhibitions, guided activities and family-oriented elements, offering a low-cost way to move between national history, local memory and contemporary artistic interpretation. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx62.text: Image source, Wild Ireland press handout Image caption, Tyapa (left) and Bu (right) were previously kept in small cages in the Republic of Dagestan in Russia By Mike McBride BBC News NI Published 25 October 2026, 00:02 BST After years in cramped cages, two brown bears are adjusting to their new life following a remarkable rescue mission that spanned multiple countries, was disrupted by two major conflicts and involved more than 100 people. For Bu and Tyapa, the five-year rescue journey from the Republic of Dagestan in Russia to the Irish countryside was anything but straightforward. One bear had spent their life forced to perform in a circus, while the other was confined to a cage so small they could not stand upright. Today, the bears are now adjusting to a totally different world among the trees and grass at Wild Ireland, a sanctuary for rescued animals in County Donegal. Image caption, Tyapa is slowly settling into her new surroundings in Burnfoot, County Donegal Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin first learned about Bu and Tyapa in 2021 and committed to bringing them to safety in Donegal. The sanctuary, located in Burnfoot, opened in October 2019 and provides a safe space for animals, including brown bears, monkeys, wolves, and lynx. Image caption, Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin says the bears' health improvements since their arrival have been remarkable McLaughlin said the two bears were in extremely poor health when they were first rescued. Former circus bear Bu had spent years confined to a small indoor cage after being forced to perform. McLaughlin said Tyapa had lived in a cage measuring just 2.5m by 2.5m by 2m, which was too low for him to stand upright and had no roof, which left him exposed to the harsh winters and blistering summer heat. The bear had no water dish and relied on a hose for drinking water. McLaughlin said he was being raised to be killed for an eventual taxidermy display. When the bears were rescued, both were severely malnourished and showed signs of psychological trauma. Blood tests also revealed serious kidney problems associated with prolonged dehydration. How do you transport two large bears? Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 made the original transport route through Ukraine impossible, said McLaughlin. An alternative route through the Middle East was then explored, but plans were disrupted again in February 2026 when the escalating conflict involving Iran led to airspace closures and flight disruptions across the region. More than 100 people were involved in the rescue operation, including volunteers, lawyers, veterinarians, animal transport specialists, cargo teams and officials in Russia, the United Arab Emirates and Ireland. Image source, Wild Ireland press handout Image caption, The bears travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in the Republic of Ireland on 3 August 2026 In late October 2025, Dima and Yana Kim, who work at Tiger House, a sanctuary near St Petersburg that cares for former circus tigers, embarked on a 36-hour drive to Dagestan to rescue the bears. Bu and Tyapa had to be cut out of their rusting steel cages, sedated and placed in secure transport crates for the journey back to Tiger House, where they received veterinary treatment and underwent quarantine. After months of preparation and repeated delays, the bears eventually travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in Ireland in August. Health improvements since arriving Since arriving at Wild Ireland, McLaughlin said both bears have gained weight, their coats have improved, and follow-up blood tests have shown that their kidney function has returned to normal. He said their habitat provides woodland, water and room to explore, as well as sheltered areas where they can retreat or move out of public view if they would like some privacy. "These bears have suffered trauma and the first step of that recovery process is get them back out into the forest, get their paws into the soil and on the grass and get them exploring. "We hope they can now have a full and happy life." Working with bears isn't your normal 9-5 Working with bears is certainly not your everyday job, but for Wild Ireland team member Chloe McElhatton, it's one she absolutely relishes. Chloe has been working at Wild Ireland for just over a year. She studied zoology at Queen's University Belfast, completing a four-year degree before joining the team. "This is obviously a very unique job, and it's quite different from what most people would do," she said. Image caption, Chloe McElhatton is part of the bear team at Wild Ireland and says looking after bears is not your average 9-5 job "We've done a lot of work hiding food around the bear habitats, encouraging them to search and forage for it themselves and this promotes their natural behaviours and helps them become more comfortable in that new open space," she said. "Over time, we've seen their confidence build, and you can see great changes, both physically and mentally, in both of them." What do visitors think of the bears? Image caption, Liam, who is from France, says the two bears are big and impressive Liam, who is from France, said the bears were one of his favourite animals to see when visiting the park. "Very big and very impressive," is how he summed up Bu and Tyapa. "I saw chickens, some wolves and some monkeys and then the bears which were definitely my favourite." Image caption, Chris Roberts is a regular visitor to Wild Ireland and came to visit hoping to see a glimpse of the two new bears Chris Roberts is from Manorcunningham, about 20 minutes from Wild Ireland, and has been visiting the site ever since it first opened in 2019. "I've lost count of how many times we've been here, but we really wanted to come down today to see if we could catch a glimpse of Bu and Tyapa. "It was fantastic to see them in the flesh. "We absolutely loved it and are delighted to see them doing so well, especially considering their backstory and the awful conditions they were once kept in."
